desc:
The arrays a and b are each sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain repeated values. Count the index pairs (i, j) with a[i] + b[j] == target. Two pairs are different if their indices differ, even when the values are equal.

a = [1, 1, 2, 4]
b = [3, 3, 5, 6]
target = 7
result = 5

The pairs are 1 + 6 (two choices of the 1), 2 + 5, and 4 + 3 (two choices of the 3): five pairs in total.
constraints: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Checking all n · m pairs is up to 25 million operations and ignores the sorted order. A hash map of counts works, but there is an O(1) memory way.
Start with a pointer i at the beginning of a and j at the end of b. If the sum is too small, only advancing i can raise it; if too large, only decreasing j can lower it.

When the sum equals the target, count how many equal values a has at i (run length x) and how many equal values b has at j (run length y). They contribute x * y pairs. Then move both pointers past those runs.
editorial: This is the classic two-sum two-pointer walk, but across two arrays and with duplicates. Place i at the smallest of a and j at the largest of b. If a[i] + b[j] < target, then a[i] is too small to pair with b[j] or with anything smaller in b, so a[i] is finished: advance i. If the sum is larger, b[j] is too large for a[i] and for everything bigger in a: decrease j.

When the sum hits the target, let x be the number of consecutive entries of a equal to a[i] and y the number of consecutive entries of b equal to b[j]. Every combination of one of them with one of the others is a valid pair, so add x * y and step both pointers beyond the runs. Counting the runs makes total work linear: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space. The answer can reach 25,000,000, which fits in 32 bits.
